job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Adam Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings I'm at the kitchen table in Ashgrove, with my parents' pharmacy two streets away. I send applications to accounting and audit firms, usually 5 or 6 a week, written carefully and checked twice. After lunch I sometimes help my father with the pharmacy's stock sheets, which he'd like to become my job. I finished accounting at Eastvale University last summer with a pass and no internship. I don't use AI tools, I'd rather do it by hand and be sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's what I expected. Some tasks get quicker, the rest stays the same. I'd tell friends that nobody should panic or celebrate yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still be uneasy, because the job hunt is slow and I'm the only one of my friends without an offer. Dad's pharmacy is a fallback, and I'm grateful, but I trained to do audit, not stock counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, 5 or 6 a week, and I'd widen it to smaller firms, because the big ones filter hard. I'd also ask my old tutor for an introduction. I'd work two days a week at the pharmacy to cover my phone and train fares, and keep the rest of my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, to be honest. Not scared, but I don't like waiting. It feels like time passing without anything counting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your father's offer is on the table. Does that make this easier or harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier to wait, so I don't panic. Harder to push, because the pharmacy is a comfortable fallback and I could stay there for years. That's a real risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you say yes to him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I had a signed offer from an audit firm and a clear training route to qualify. If I get to year two without that, I'll say yes to Dad, and I'd be fine with it, just not proud.

do: Keep applying, **5 or 6**, and widen it to smaller firms.

Work **two days** a week at the pharmacy to cover small costs.
feel: A bit **flat**, since waiting feels like time passing without counting.

fieldNote: The **comfortable fallback** is both his safety net and his worry.
He is measured and sets himself a **two-year** limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not a revolution, but it will change the first years of accounting. I wouldn't claim to know how much. I'd tell people to watch the actual hiring numbers, not the headlines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it worries me. Checking invoices and matching ledgers is exactly the work that new accountants do, and software is good at it. I haven't used AI tools, and I know that could count against me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably try one tool, in a careful way, maybe the one my tutor suggests. I'd also take on the pharmacy's books properly, and offer to do the books for two other small shops on our street. That gives me something real to show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit. I'm comfortable doing things by hand, and I don't like being rushed. But it's not panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of audit work would software take over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Invoice matching, bank reconciliations, sampling transactions for audit, even drafting basic reports. In a normal firm the first-year juniors do those. Several firms I applied to said they're reviewing how many trainees to take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change how you work, or wait and see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait and see is more my style. I like to see something proven before trusting it. But with this, waiting could cost me the first job, so I'll go partly against my nature and try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and no one is ready, including governments and firms. I'd say it plainly and not blame any one group, because honestly everybody is surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be afraid my degree is worth nothing. Accounting is thinking work, and if software does it cheaper, firms stop hiring juniors. I'd have trained for a job that closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay home and take the pharmacy job full time, because it's the one thing I know is safe. I'd cut every unneeded expense and keep six months of savings. I'd also ask if the pharmacy can do more services, since people will always need medicine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's like finding out the road you've been walking ends. I'd be quiet about it, which is my way, but my mum would notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain this to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit them down and say what I've said here, calmly and with numbers. Dad would say the pharmacy will always be there, and Mum would worry. And I'd say, I know, but I'd like to find something of my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first bill you'd protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pharmacy's supplier bill, because that keeps the shop open for the whole family. After that, my own phone and train costs.

I wouldn't blame one group, because everyone is surprised.
think: I'm afraid my **degree** is worth nothing, since accounting is thinking work.
Firms stop hiring juniors, so I'd have trained for a job that closes.

fieldNote: Alarm is **quiet** but real; he expects the junior accounting door to close.

steps.text: Take the full-time job at my father's pharmacy

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short, but it's something. We could use it to retrain people. I'd say there shouldn't be panic, but there should be planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious but manageable. If I land a job in the next year, I'd have a few years to become useful beyond the routine tasks. If I don't, the pharmacy is there, and I could study.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first audit or finance job I can get, even a small one. I'd learn the AI tools there, with someone showing me, since I'm slow alone. I'd save as much as possible and avoid big purchases until 2031 is clearer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a countdown I can see, which is better than a surprise. But it's still a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes, but I'd aim for the human parts: advice, judgement, explaining numbers to owners. The pharmacy gives me a good example, people trust my dad because they know him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to be an accountant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a shock. Five lets me avoid a shock. It's not nothing, but it doesn't remove the worry.

say: Five years is short, but it's something to use for **retraining**.
There should be no panic, but there should be **planning**.
think: If I land a job soon I'd have time to become useful beyond **routine tasks**.
If not, the pharmacy is there.
do: Take the first **audit or finance job** I can get, even a small one.

feel: **Uneasy**, since a visible countdown is better than a surprise but is still a countdown.
S3.quote: Two years is a shock. Five lets me avoid a shock.
fieldNote: He values **warning** over reassurance, which suits his careful style.
Plans to learn AI with a mentor, accepting he is **slow alone**.
Aims for human-facing parts: advice and explaining numbers.

steps.text: Take the first small audit or finance job offered
Learn the AI tools with a colleague showing me
Save hard and avoid big purchases until 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's enough time if people use it sensibly. Governments should be clear about the plan now. I'd wait for details before saying more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be mostly fine. I'd be 33 by then, with years of experience and probably a family. The world would have changed several times over, so it's not a single cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a first job, qualify as a chartered accountant, which takes about three years, and learn the tools step by step. I'd take over the pharmacy's finances alongside. And I'd save toward a house deposit instead of waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. It's far enough away that I can plan, and near enough that I won't forget it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so. I like checklists. I'd put a review in my diary every January and ask whether the plan still works. I wouldn't use the time to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you believe you'd actually use the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My honest answer is that I'd take the long view. Slow and steady has been my approach, and with ten years it's the right approach.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years isn't enough for firms, governments or me to react, and I'd be stuck choosing the pharmacy by default. What would help is a clear plan from government early, trainee places protected at firms, and someone showing people like me the tools step by step.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I just don't like being rushed. If I'm shown something proven, I'll use it, and I'd rather be a careful accountant than a fast one.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change. I just don't like being rushed.
portrait: Adam is a **23-year-old** accounting graduate living in Ashgrove, applying carefully and helping at his parents' pharmacy.
He is **centre** and blames no one group; he prefers evidence over headlines.
He is **resistant** to new tools, avoids AI and admits that may cost him a first job.
The pharmacy gives him a **fallback**, but it quietly worries him as a comfortable trap.
He becomes alarmed in the 2028 world and plans steadily when there is a long runway.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028**, where juniors stop being hired and the pharmacy becomes his default.
whatWouldHelp: A **clear government plan** early, protected trainee places, and someone showing him the tools step by step.
